title: NVIDIA Vera Storage Benchmarks: Faster Encryption, Compression, Integrity Checking, and Recovery for AI-Native Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA publishes its own microbenchmarks showing the 88-core Arm-based Vera CPU inside the BlueField-4 STX Storage Processor beating an unnamed x86 CPU by 1.29x-3.67x across encryption, Reed-Solomon recovery, CRC32C, compression, and a two-stage compression-plus-encryption write pipeline (3.21x). The strategic move is extending the same Vera CPU architecture that hosts Rubin GPUs into the storage data path, framing agentic AI as a CPU-side storage-processing problem and targeting the x86 server CPU installed base in storage arrays.

themes.theme: Agentic AI as a storage-CPU problem

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames the binding constraint in agentic AI infrastructure as CPU-side storage processing, arguing that inference runs on GPUs but agentic processes, tool calls, data management, and supporting storage services all run on CPUs.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: This reframing expands NVIDIA's addressable silicon from the accelerator socket into the storage controller and host CPU sockets that Intel and AMD currently own.
insights.quote: AI inference runs on GPUs, but agentic processes, tool calls, data management tasks, and the storage services that support them run on CPUs.
insights.locator: Each agent step can trigger multiple storage operations

insights.claim: Agent workloads multiply storage operations combinatorially — each agent step triggers multiple storage operations, repeated across thousands of concurrent agents with growing context windows — so storage load scales faster than user count.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Storage I/O per dollar of inference revenue rises with agent adoption; that is the demand curve for AI-native storage vendors.
insights.quote: Each agent step can trigger multiple storage operations, and those operations can repeat across thousands of concurrent agents with increasingly larger context windows.
insights.locator: Storage is an active part of every agentic AI workflow

insights.claim: Faster SSDs and networks deliver no benefit if the processor securing, protecting, and preparing the data cannot keep pace, making the storage CPU rather than the media the limiting stage in the data path.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: A direct argument against buying faster NAND without upgrading the storage processor — relevant to how storage array vendors position next refresh cycles.
insights.quote: Faster SSDs and networks cannot deliver their full potential if the processor securing, protecting, and preparing the data cannot keep pace.
insights.locator: Many of these functions sit directly in the data path

insights.claim: Scaling storage data services on conventional CPUs requires more cores, power, and cooling while leaving performance gated by the slowest step in the pipeline, converting a throughput problem into a datacenter facilities cost problem.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Power and cooling envelopes, not capex, are increasingly the constraint on AI datacenter buildout — favoring Arm-based efficiency plays.
insights.locator: Scaling them with conventional CPUs

insights.claim: The Vera CPU packs 88 NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores fully compatible with the Armv9.2 instruction set and supports 176 threads via NVIDIA Spatial Multithreading.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: A custom 88-core Arm server CPU shipping into storage controllers is a direct competitive datapoint against x86 server share; Arm ISA lock-in also matters for software ecosystems.
insights.quote: Vera CPU includes 88 NVIDIA-designed Olympus CPU cores that are fully compatible with the Armv9.2 instruction set.
insights.locator: Vera CPU architecture: Built for storage's dual demands

insights.claim: The NVIDIA Scalable Coherency Fabric provides up to 3.4 TB/s of bisection bandwidth with a 164 MB unified L3 cache across cores, shared cache, memory controllers, and I/O.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: 164 MB unified L3 and 3.4 TB/s on-die bandwidth are the specs that make streaming crypto and compression workloads cache-resident — the mechanism behind the benchmark wins.
insights.locator: The SCF provides a coherent, on-die data path

insights.claim: SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory supplies up to 1.2 TB/s aggregate bandwidth or up to 14 GB/s per core, and NVIDIA emphasizes it is modular and field-replaceable rather than soldered.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: LPDDR5X displacing DDR5 RDIMMs in datacenter sockets shifts memory demand toward mobile-DRAM supply lines — a mix shift for memory makers and module vendors.
insights.quote: up to 1.2 TB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth, or up to 14 GB/s per core
insights.locator: The SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory subsystem

insights.claim: NVIDIA identifies storage primitives as imposing two distinct and simultaneous CPU demands — sustained per-core latency within a stream, plus bandwidth and predictable latency across many concurrent streams — a framework explaining why generic core-count scaling fails.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for evaluating any storage-processor claim: ask whether the vendor solved the serial-latency side or only the throughput side.
insights.locator: Storage primitives place two distinct demands on a CPU

insights.claim: The Olympus core is described as combining wide instruction throughput, advanced branch prediction, deep out-of-order execution, and dedicated vector and cryptographic resources — a general-purpose high-IPC design rather than a fixed-function offload engine.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Programmable cores beat fixed-function ASICs when algorithms churn; this is a bet that storage data services will keep evolving.
insights.locator: Vera addresses both requirements

insights.claim: Every reported result is a memory-resident single-process microbenchmark that explicitly excludes file I/O, disk performance, networking, command startup, and external-device bottlenecks — measuring CPU headroom, not delivered storage-system performance.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: The headline multiples are ceilings under ideal conditions; real array throughput will land materially lower, so do not model revenue impact off these ratios.
insights.quote: The tests exclude file I/O, disk performance, networking, command startup, and external-device bottlenecks unless otherwise identified.
insights.locator: Measuring foundational storage performance

insights.claim: NVIDIA concedes the benchmark suite is not an off-the-shelf public benchmark, and the x86 comparison part is never named anywhere in the post.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: An unnamed baseline plus a house-built suite is the classic pattern for vendor-favorable comparisons; wait for third-party or SPEC-style validation before treating the gaps as durable.
insights.quote: although the complete benchmark set is not an off-the-shelf public benchmark
insights.locator: A purpose-built test framework runs each workload

insights.claim: NVIDIA itself states that end-to-end testing is still required to quantify complete storage-system or GPU-performance outcomes, an unusually explicit disclaimer inside a performance-marketing post.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: The hedge signals that the primitive-level wins have not yet been demonstrated to convert into array-level wins — the key thing to watch from storage OEM partners.
insights.quote: End-to-end testing is still required to quantify complete storage-system or GPU-performance outcomes.
insights.locator: When combined in production storage software

insights.claim: The comparison uses common libraries including OpenSSL, Zstandard, and LZ4 with implementations optimized for native instructions on both Arm and x86, which is the strongest fairness claim in the methodology.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Using standard libraries limits the usual 'unoptimized baseline' criticism, making these numbers more credible than typical vendor benchmarks.
insights.locator: The benchmark set uses common libraries

insights.claim: Vera delivers up to 1.43x higher AES-128 encryption throughput and up to 1.29x higher AES-128 decryption throughput than the comparison x86 CPU — the narrowest margins in the entire benchmark set.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Crypto is where x86 has mature dedicated instructions, so the sub-1.5x margin here is the honest read on Vera's general per-core advantage.
insights.locator: Securing more AI data with faster encryption

insights.claim: Vera shows up to 3.26x higher Reed-Solomon throughput than x86 in a recovery workload, targeting rebuild and degraded-read paths rather than the write-path encoding path.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Shorter rebuild windows reduce the exposure period where a second drive failure loses data — a real reliability argument for large flash fleets, not just a speed number.
insights.quote: Vera delivers up to 3.26x higher Reed-Solomon throughput than the x86 CPU in a recovery workload.
insights.locator: Protecting and recovering AI data faster

insights.claim: CRC32C integrity checking is the single largest measured gap at up to 3.67x over x86, a function storage systems run on both read and write paths and even while copying between buffers.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: The highest-frequency, lowest-glamour operation showing the biggest gap is where aggregate CPU savings actually accumulate in production.
insights.locator: Validating data integrity at higher throughput

insights.claim: Compression throughput runs up to 3.29x higher than x86 while decompression reaches only 1.72x, and NVIDIA notes the decompression advantage widens as more worker threads run in parallel.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: The asymmetry matters: compression is deferrable, decompression sits in the latency-critical read path where the advantage is nearly half as large.
insights.quote: Vera delivers up to 1.72x higher decompression throughput than the x86 CPU under concurrency, with its advantage increasing as more worker threads run in parallel.
insights.locator: The decompression benchmark measures

insights.claim: NVIDIA explicitly hedges that compression results vary by algorithm, data characteristics, compression level, buffer size, and thread count and apply specifically to the measured workloads.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Compression is the most tunable and therefore most cherry-pickable benchmark in the set; treat the 3.29x as configuration-specific.
insights.locator: Compression performance varies by algorithm

insights.claim: A two-stage memory-resident pipeline applying compression then encryption to each buffer runs up to 3.21x faster on Vera than x86, showing the advantage compounds rather than collapses when operations are chained.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: This is the most decision-relevant number since production write paths always chain operations; it beats the standalone encryption figure of 1.43x, implying memory-subsystem advantages dominate over per-primitive ones.
insights.quote: Vera delivers up to 3.21x higher pipeline throughput than the x86 CPU used in the benchmark for the two-stage compression and encryption pipeline.
insights.locator: Accelerating a multi-stage storage write path

themes.theme: One CPU architecture across compute and storage

insights.claim: The same Vera CPU architecture designed to keep NVIDIA Rubin GPUs fed is being reused inside BlueField-4 STX for storage-path processing, giving NVIDIA a single core design amortized across host compute and storage infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Design reuse across two large sockets improves NVIDIA's return on CPU R&D and squeezes the merchant DPU and storage-controller silicon market.
insights.quote: The same Vera CPU architecture designed to keep NVIDIA Rubin GPUs fed also accelerates the CPU-side storage processing.
insights.locator: Closing the storage processing gap

insights.claim: Standalone Vera is claimed to deliver up to 1.8x higher performance per core in agentic tools, a figure asserted without benchmark detail inside a post otherwise dense with methodology.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: A 1.8x per-core claim against x86 in general agentic workloads is the broader competitive threat; its lack of supporting detail here is the tell to watch for elsewhere.
insights.quote: Standalone Vera delivers up to 1.8x higher performance per core in agentic tools.
insights.locator: Scaling agent execution and storage with Vera

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims higher measured performance per watt across selected workloads, positioning power efficiency rather than raw speed as the purchasing argument in power-constrained AI factories.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: The qualifier 'across selected workloads' is doing heavy lifting; still, perf/watt is the metric that decides deployments once grid power caps rack density.
insights.quote: Across selected workloads, Vera also delivers higher measured performance per watt
insights.locator: By sustaining these functions individually

insights.claim: The final pitch is a common CPU architecture and software toolchain spanning both agent execution and the supporting data infrastructure, extending NVIDIA's software-lock-in model from CUDA on GPUs to the CPU and storage layers.
insights.speaker: Jason Hardy
insights.so_what: Toolchain unification across compute and storage is the moat play; the risk to competitors is being designed out of the AI factory reference architecture entirely.
insights.quote: A common Vera CPU architecture and software toolchain across compute and storage provides a consistent foundation for scaling both agent execution and the supporting data infrastructure.
insights.locator: A common Vera CPU architecture
